dataset.name: SPRUCE S1 Bog Pretreatment Seasonal Photosynthesis and Respiration of Trees, Shrubs, and Herbaceous Plants, 2010-2015
description: This data set contains the empirical biochemical, morphological, and physiological data collected between 2010 and 2015 on an herb (Maianthemum trifolium), understory shrubs (Rhododendron groenlandicum, Chamaedaphne calyculata, Kalmia polifolia and Vaccinium angustifolium) and overstory trees (Picea mariana and Larix laricina) in the S1-Bog at the USDA Forest Service Marcell Experimental Forest (MEF) in northern Minnesota, USA. Data reported include the measurements of photosynthetic light and CO2 response curves, and dark respiration, as applied to standardized curve-fitting programs to estimate biochemical parameters. These data were collected prior to the initiating of heating and elevation of CO2 for the SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) experiment in the S1-Bog to assess the response of northern peatland ecosystems to increases in temperature and exposures to elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations.

measurementTechnique:
Site Description:
The site is the 8.1-ha S1 bog, a Picea mariana [black spruce] – Sphagnum spp. ombrotrophic bog forest in northern Minnesota, 40 km north of Grand Rapids, in the USDA Forest Service Marcell Experimental Forest (MEF). The S1 bog was harvested in successive strip cuts in 1969 and 1974 and the cut areas were allowed to naturally regenerate. The 1974 strips are characterized by medium density of 3-6 meter black spruce and larch trees with an open canopy. The 1969 harvest strips are characterized by a higher density of 3-6 meter black spruce and larch trees with a generally closed canopy.

Materials and Methods:
Seasonal patterns of the photosynthetic capacity of current year foliage were measured during field campaigns in June, July, August, September, and October between 2010 and 2015. Samples were collected randomly throughout the southern half of the S1 bog
Sampling
Samples were collected from the sunlit middle/upper canopy of the overstory trees (P. mariana and L. laricina), dominant understory shrubs (R. groenlandicum, C. calyculata), sub-dominant shrub (K. polifolia, V. angustifolium) and the herbaceous layer (M. trifolium).
• Samples were cut, then immediately recut underwater and maintained fully hydrated during measurement.
• Measurement logistics depended on phenology, weather, equipment and personnel availability; not all species were measured at each field campaign.

Photosynthesis and Respiration Measurements
We measured photosynthetic light and CO2 response (A/Ci) curves and dark respiration (Rd) using portable infrared gas analyzer systems (LI6400XT, Li-COR, USA).
Photosynthesis
• Light response (A/Q) curves were measured at ambient CO2 concentration ([CO2] = 400 ppm) during sequential reduction in light levels from 1600 to 0 μmol photons m-2 s-1; n = 3-6 replicates per species per month.
• A/Ci curves were at saturated light levels (PAR = 1000 μmol photons m-2 s-1) by sequential adjustment of the reference CO2 concentration between 50 and 1600 ppm (400, 300, 200, 100, 50, 400, 550, 650, 800, 950, 1200, 1600 ppm) after first acclimating the sample at 400 ppm until stable; n = 3-10 replicates per month per species.
• Each curve typically took 25-30 min to complete.
• All curves used the 2 x 3 cm measurement chamber.
Due to multi-year cohorts on the Picea, some foliage was removed by clipping to accommodate the gas exchange chamber gasket (Figure 2).
We minimized variations in VPD by regulating humidity manually, prior to, but not during, the automated A/Q and A/Ci curve measurements. Curves were measured within ~10°C of ambient Tair by adjusting the block temperature to 15-18°C (Sept), 20°C (Oct) or 25°C (June-Aug) during each field campaign; resulting in Tleaf 11-28°C (A/Q) and 13-29°C (A/Ci). Analysis was based on one-sided projected leaf area for all species, estimated using WinRHIZO 2012b (Regent Instruments Canada Inc., Canada) and ImageJ 1.47 (U. S. National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, Maryland, USA) software.
Respiration
• Temperature responses of foliar daytime Rd were measured from 2 to 50°C by Peltier adjustment and use of a temperature-controlled recirculating water bath attached to the cuvette with block water-jackets.
• Rates were recorded 5-10 min. after target temperatures were reached.
• Temperature response curves of foliar Rd were collected from P. mariana and R. groenlandicum during June/July (2014) and September (2013).
• We calculated foliar Rd Q10 values according to Linder and Troeng (1981).
Seasonal values of Rd were compiled from A/Q curves and adjusted to rates at 25°C using temperature response functions for P. mariana, and R. groenlandicum. We assumed similar temperature responses across season and standardized the rates of respiration for trees and shrubs using temperature response functions for P. mariana and R. groenlandicum, respectively. The M. trifolium, being an understory species, was assumed to have the same temperature response as R. groenlandicum.

A/Ci Curve Analyses
A/Ci curves were analyzed with the LeafWeb online tool and database (http://leafweb.ornl.gov), which uses an automated, objective exhaustive dual optimization approach to choose curve points and fit parameters to the Farquhar-von Caemmerer-Berry model (Gu et al. 2010).
• Parameters include estimates of the maximum rate of Rubisco carboxylation (Vcmax25C), maximum electron transport (Jmax25C), maximum triose phosphate utilization (VTPU25°C) and daytime dark respiration (RD25°C), all normalized to 25°C based on Bernacchi et al. (2002).
• Light response curves were fitted according to Ye (2007) using a spreadsheet tool (Lobo et al. (2013)) to obtain maximum gross photosynthetic rate (Agmax), light compensation point (Icomp) and quantum yield between Icomp and I = 200 μmol(photon) m–2 s–1 from each A/Q curve.
• Raw gas exchange data is available upon request.

Leaf Physical and Chemical Characterization
Leaf mass per area was derived from resultant leaf area and tissue dry weight. Tissue was dried at 70°C then analyzed for leaf carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) content using an elemental analyzer (Costech Analytical Technologies, Inc., USA).
